Emergency Action Protocol
Did You Just Feel an Earthquake?
Follow these three vital directives immediately to protect yourself and your family.
1. Drop, Cover, & Hold On
Drop to your hands and knees immediately. Cover your head and neck beneath a sturdy desk or table. Hold on until the shaking completely stops. Do not run outdoors during shaking.
Complete Survival Guide
2. Check Utilities & Hazards
Once shaking ceases, inspect your surroundings. If you smell gas or hear hissing, turn off the main valve and evacuate immediately. Watch out for shattered glass and downed electrical lines.
Home Hazard Checklists
3. Prepare for Aftershocks
Moderate-to-severe earthquakes are invariably followed by aftershock sequences. Keep your sturdy shoes, emergency go-bag, and flashlight beside your bed or exit door.
Aftershock Safety Rules
Seismological Physics
How Seismic Waves Travel to Your Location
When tectonic fault planes rupture underground, seismic energy radiates outward in distinct wave packets. Understanding these wave velocities explains why shaking feels different across varying distances.
5 to 8 km/s
First to Arrive
Primary (P) Waves
Compressional waves that travel through solid crust and liquid mantle. They arrive first and are typically perceived as an abrupt vertical thump or rattling windows rather than violent rolling.
3 to 4.5 km/s
Second to Arrive
Secondary (S) Waves
Shear waves that oscillate perpendicular to propagation direction. Traveling only through solid rock, S-waves arrive seconds after P-waves, generating intense horizontal shear shaking.
2 to 4 km/s
Most Destructive
Surface Waves (Love & Rayleigh)
Trapped near the Earth's surface, these waves exhibit massive vertical elliptical rolling and transverse shearing. They diminish slowly with distance and cause maximum structural strain.
Early warning systems leverage the P-to-S time interval to send alerts before damaging shear waves arrive.
Read Full Seismic Wave Analysis
Understanding Seismic Metrics
Why Local Shaking Intensity Differs from Magnitude
A common misconception is that magnitude alone defines how much shaking you will experience. In reality, what you feel at your exact location is governed by three critical factors:
Factor 1
Epicenter Distance
Seismic wave amplitude attenuates exponentially as energy spreads geometrically through the crust. Double the distance often reduces felt intensity by over 75%.
Factor 2
Focal Depth
Shallow earthquakes (0–15 km deep) focus violent energy directly beneath surface structures, whereas deep earthquakes (100+ km) dissipate energy across broad territories.
Factor 3
Local Soil Resonance
Soft alluvial soils and reclaimed land amplify seismic waves significantly compared to solid bedrock, occasionally triggering liquefaction during prolonged tremors.
